items.title: Jimmy Heath interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, September 8, 2014
items.q: I knew when Trane could play ballads and touch people you know.

ctx.x: — but it was created by African-Americans. And there were a few whites, even at that time, you know, Bix Beiderbecke and people back there, they were in that same mode. But the majority of the performers were African-Americans. Now all over the world there are people — you know I’ve been all over and I hear people playing like Sonny Rollins or Coltrane or Dizzy or whoever, from here, coming from all over the world. They’ve heard that music and they’ve absorbed some of the improvisational language.
Do you consider yourself — you grew up in the bebop era.

items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I told about Coltrane and I, with Dizzy and we’d go to the Riverside Theatre in Milwaukee. We were opening the next day, so we both loved Jimmy Dorsey’s alto saxophone playing because we were both playing altos, at the time, in Dizzy’s band.

ctx.x: Yeah. I’ve been stuck this year listening to Delius, Frederick Delius. He’s like, for lack of another word, I like romantic, I like melodic. The romantic era: Debussey, and Ravel, he’s in that bag, Frederick Delius. I’ve been listening, in retrospect, to, I’ve got some recordings by a company called Chronolgical Classics from France. I’ve got five C.D.’s of Jimmy Lunceford’s band. I haven’t talked to Wynton since we did the thing with Willie Nelson, with Cosby. I have to tell him he’s been doing everybody but…

it when I was a kid. I heard all the big bands, I heard Tommy Dorsey when “I’ll never smile again” (Imitates Dorsey). All that, you know when Frankie was there. Being around the giants of music, and I told a lot of these stories that are going to be in this documentation, in my book.
